summary: The canonical format of the RFC Series is changing from plain-text ASCII to XML using the xml2rfc version 3 vocabulary, with other formats rendered from that. This informational document gives the framework that ties together the specifications for the various formats. It was replaced by RFC 9720.

plainLanguage.summary: RFCs used to be plain typed text. They are moving to a richer source from which nice versions are made. This is the big-picture plan. It was replaced by RFC 9720.

subtitle: Transitioning RFCs from plain text ASCII to XML for richer publishing.

tldr.problem: The plain-text ASCII format for RFCs limits readability and cannot represent non-ASCII characters or complex layouts suitable for modern devices.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7990 establishes a framework to transition RFCs to use XML as the canonical format with xml2rfc v3 vocabulary, from which HTML, PDF, and plain text are rendered.
tldr.outcome: This framework document was superseded by RFC 9720, which provides updated guidance on the RFC format transition.

today: RFC 7990 has been obsoleted by RFC 9720, which provides updated guidance on the RFC format transition.

sections.title: Why Change the RFC Format
sections.content:
The RFC Series has used plain-text ASCII format since its beginning. This format was archival and accessible but has limitations. Billions of people now access the Internet from diverse devices and locations, and they need RFCs to be viewable on phones, tablets, and computers with proper formatting. Author names with non-Latin characters cannot be represented in ASCII. Complex diagrams and artwork become hard to read in plain text.

RFC 7990 provides the framework for a transition from plain-text ASCII to a new format. The canonical, authoritative version of an RFC will be XML using the xml2rfc v3 vocabulary. From this XML source, the RFC Editor will generate multiple publication formats: HTML, PDF/A-3, plain text UTF-8, and potentially EPUB. This keeps the RFC archival while allowing rich presentation to modern readers.
sections.plainLanguage: Old RFCs were just plain text because that worked everywhere. Now they are written in a format that can be turned into a nice website or PDF, with the plain text version still available for people who want it.

sections.title: The New Format Architecture
sections.content:
The RFC Editor will create files in three layers. The canonical format is XML using xml2rfc v3, containing all the information an RFC needs. This version is signed and archived as the official record. Publication formats are the versions people read: HTML rendered for modern browsers with JavaScript for errata and metadata, PDF/A-3 for long-term storage and legal compliance, and UTF-8 plain text for backward compatibility and legacy tools.

SVG artwork will be supported and embedded in the XML. The XML file will contain automatically generated identifiers for sections, figures, tables, and paragraphs so that links are stable. Authors may submit drafts in xml2rfc v2 or plain text, but the RFC Editor will convert to v3 XML for publication. The final XML will be self-contained with all external features expanded inline.
sections.plainLanguage: The source document is XML, which is like a structured instruction book. From that, computers create three different versions: a pretty HTML website, a PDF that lasts forever, and plain text for old computers.

sections.title: Content and Design Goals
sections.content:
The RFC Series must remain archival and accessible. Legal and technical teams must be able to rely on RFCs for compliance and reference. The new format must preserve this. The HTML version will use Cascading Style Sheets to be reflowable on different screen sizes and allow CSS overrides by readers. JavaScript will be limited to adding post-publication metadata and errata pointers; it cannot modify the RFC text itself.

The RFC Style Guide was updated to focus on content, structure, and grammar rather than page formatting. New specifications define HTML semantics, PDF tagging for accessibility, CSS requirements, SVG artwork profiles, and rules for non-ASCII characters in RFCs. All these documents (RFC 7992 for HTML, RFC 7994 for plain text, RFC 7995 for PDF, RFC 7996 for SVG, RFC 7997 for non-ASCII) provide the detailed requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: The new versions must still be trustworthy for lawyers and engineers. The HTML can look nice on any device. Special rules make sure RFCs are accessible and readable for years to come.

sections.title: The Transition Plan
sections.content:
The transition happens in stages. First, tool developers create new software using the xml2rfc v3 vocabulary. The RFC Editor will test with volunteer drafts, running some through the old process and new process simultaneously. Authors and the community provide feedback on the new formats. During this phase, published RFCs continue using the old process and plain-text format only.

Next, as tools mature, both old and new processes run in parallel. The RFC Editor publishes documents with both methods and collects feedback on the quality of new outputs. Authors can submit XML or plain text; if they submit plain text, the RFC Editor generates the XML. Finally, when the new tools are stable and well-tested, the old process retires. All new RFCs are published with XML as the canonical version and all formats rendered from it.

A known risk is that resource demands are hard to predict. The transition requires the RFC Production Center to support both old and new processes for months, potentially causing publication delays. Readers may see some RFCs available in all formats while older ones have only plain text.
sections.plainLanguage: The change happens slowly. First, people build the new tools and test them. Then, both old and new ways work at the same time. Finally, when everyone is ready, the old way stops and only the new way is used.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content: RFC 7990 is an Informational document published by the Internet Architecture Board and has been obsoleted by RFC 9720, which provides updated and more recent guidance on the RFC format.
sections.plainLanguage: This document was later updated by RFC 9720, which has newer information about how the format change happened and what came next.
